title: Media Literacy and Fake News
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about how to find the truth in a flood of information -- the difference between disinformation and misinformation, and the tools of source criticism.
competenceGoals: reflect critically on media literacy, source evaluation, and the spread of misinformation
analyse and assess how English-language media covers political and social issues

content.content:
## Drowning in information

Every day, millions of news articles, social media posts, videos and podcasts compete for your attention. We live in an age of *information abundance*, which sounds wonderful -- and in many ways it is, offering unprecedented access to knowledge. But it creates a fundamental challenge: how do you tell reliable information from falsehood when both arrive in the same endless scroll?

The term **fake news** entered the mainstream vocabulary during the 2016 US presidential election, but deliberately spreading false information is as old as human communication itself. What has changed is the *speed and scale* at which it now spreads. A false story can race around the world before fact-checkers have time to verify the claim. That is why **media literacy** -- the ability to critically analyse and evaluate media content -- has become one of the most important skills for any citizen in the twenty-first century. This chapter explores the mechanisms behind misinformation and the practical tools for navigating the modern information landscape.

## Three kinds of falsehood

To think clearly about fake news, you first need to separate some terms that are often confused. **Disinformation** is false information that is *deliberately* created and spread with the intent to deceive, manipulate or cause harm -- think of state-sponsored propaganda designed to destabilise other countries, fabricated news articles created for political manipulation, or doctored images and deepfake videos. **Misinformation**, by contrast, is false information shared *without* the intent to deceive -- someone passing on an outdated health claim they genuinely believe, a news outlet making an honest error later corrected, or a rumour spreading during a crisis before verified facts are available. The distinction matters because the responses differ: disinformation calls for counter-intelligence and legal measures, while misinformation calls for education and media literacy. A third category, **malinformation**, refers to genuine information shared out of context or manipulated to cause harm, such as leaking private information to damage someone's reputation.

A further reason we are vulnerable is psychological. **Confirmation bias** is the human tendency to favour information that confirms what we already believe, which makes us more likely to accept and share fake news that fits our existing views. You can see all of this in a real example. During the COVID-19 pandemic, a widely shared post claimed that 5G mobile networks caused the virus. Apply media-literacy skills and the claim falls apart: the source was anonymous conspiracy websites, not scientific institutions; no peer-reviewed study links radio waves to viral transmission, and COVID-19 spread in countries without 5G; the claim emerged during a period of fear when conspiracy theories flourish; it appealed to pre-existing distrust of technology companies, amplified by confirmation bias; and major scientific institutions and fact-checkers explicitly debunked it. The conclusion is clear -- a deliberately fabricated claim, that is, disinformation, that exploited fear to spread.

exercise.task: Test yourself on disinformation and media literacy:

questions.task: What is the difference between disinformation and misinformation?

options.text: Disinformation is deliberately spread to deceive; misinformation is shared without that intent

questions.solution: Disinformation is false information deliberately spread to deceive, while misinformation is false information shared without the intent to mislead.

options.text: The tendency to favour information that confirms existing beliefs
The tendency to reject all information

questions.solution: Confirmation bias is the human tendency to favour information that aligns with our existing beliefs, making us more vulnerable to fake news that fits our views.

options.text: Genuine information shared out of context or manipulated to cause harm

questions.solution: Malinformation is genuine information shared out of context or manipulated to cause harm, such as leaking private information to damage a reputation.

questions.task: In the 5G-COVID example, why was the claim classified as disinformation?

options.text: Because it was true but exaggerated
Because it was a deliberately fabricated claim that exploited fear to spread

questions.solution: The claim was classified as disinformation because it was deliberately fabricated, lacked any credible source or evidence, and exploited public fear to spread rapidly.

content.content:
## The toolkit of source criticism

Knowing that false information exists is not enough; you need practical tools to evaluate sources, and this is the discipline of **source criticism** -- the systematic evaluation of information sources. One widely used framework, developed by librarians at California State University, is the **CRAAP test**, an acronym that turns evaluation into five questions you can ask of almost anything you read.

*C* stands for **Currency**: how recent is the information? When was it published or last updated, and is it current enough for your topic? *R* stands for **Relevance**: does the information actually address your question, in sufficient depth and at the right level? *A* stands for **Authority**: who created the information, and are they qualified? What are the author's credentials and affiliations, and is the publisher reputable? The second *A* stands for **Accuracy**: is the information reliable and supported by evidence? Are claims backed by data, references or citations, and has the content been peer-reviewed or fact-checked? And *P* stands for **Purpose**: why was the information created -- to inform, persuade, sell or entertain -- and are there potential biases or conflicts of interest? Running a source through these five questions is a powerful habit, because it shifts you from passively absorbing content to actively interrogating it. It is also worth understanding *why* false news spreads so effectively: it is often more novel and emotionally engaging than the truth, and algorithms amplify content that provokes strong reactions. Knowing that, and having a framework like CRAAP, turns media literacy from a vague ideal into a concrete, everyday practice -- one that protects not just you, but the quality of democratic debate itself.

questions.task: What does the CRAAP test help you do?

options.text: Systematically evaluate the reliability of a source

questions.solution: The CRAAP test is a framework for systematically evaluating the reliability of an information source across five dimensions.

questions.task: What does the "A" for Authority in the CRAAP test ask?

options.text: Who created the information and whether they are qualified

questions.solution: The Authority criterion asks who created the information, what their credentials and affiliations are, and whether the publisher is reputable.

questions.task: What does the "P" for Purpose in the CRAAP test ask?

options.text: Why the information was created and whether there are biases

questions.solution: The Purpose criterion asks why the information was created -- to inform, persuade, sell or entertain -- and whether there are potential biases or conflicts of interest.

questions.task: Why does false news often spread faster than the truth?

options.text: Because it is often more novel and emotionally engaging, and algorithms amplify it
Because it is always verified first

questions.solution: False news tends to be more novel and emotionally engaging than the truth, and algorithms amplify content that provokes strong reactions, helping it spread quickly.

content.content:
## In short

In an age of information abundance, media literacy -- the ability to critically evaluate media content -- has become an essential skill. Disinformation is false information deliberately spread to deceive, misinformation is false information shared without that intent, and malinformation is genuine information manipulated to cause harm. Confirmation bias makes us vulnerable by drawing us to information that fits our existing beliefs, as the false claim linking 5G to COVID-19 showed. The CRAAP test -- Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose -- offers a practical framework for evaluating any source. Because false news spreads fast through novelty, emotion and algorithmic amplification, these tools matter not only for individuals but for the health of democratic debate.
